title: Job 42:1–6
context: Job answers the LORD a second time, after the speeches from the whirlwind (38:1–41:34), confessing, “I know that you can do all things,” and admitting that he has spoken of things too wonderful for him. He recalls the LORD’s own questions to him and says, “I had heard of you by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye sees you,” before his final words in 42:6, which translators and interpreters render and explain in several ways. Both traditions read this as Job’s humble response to God’s self-revelation, not as an admission that the friends were right, and both hold together his confession here with the LORD’s commendation that follows in 42:7.

verses.arminianNotes:
“Then Job answered the LORD.” Arminian readers note that this is Job’s second reply to the LORD, after his brief answer in 40:3–5.

The speaker is Job, now addressing God directly rather than the friends.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see Job turning from argument with the friends to response before God.

Shared ground: both traditions name Job as the speaker and read his words as an answer to the LORD’s speeches, not as a reply to Eliphaz, Bildad, or Zophar.

verses.text: “I know that you can do all things, and that no purpose of yours can be restrained.
verses.arminianNotes:
“I know that you can do all things, and that no purpose of yours can be restrained.” Arminian readers note that Job confesses God’s power and purpose.

They read the confession as compatible with God’s freely chosen ways of working with human beings.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise hear a confession that God’s purposes stand, and many in this tradition connect it with God’s sovereign counsel.

Shared ground: both traditions take the verse as a true confession of God’s power and faithfulness, spoken by Job after God has spoken.

verses.text: You asked, ‘Who is this who hides counsel without knowledge?’ therefore I have uttered that which I didn’t understand, things too wonderful for me, which I didn’t know.
verses.arminianNotes:
Job recalls the LORD’s question, “Who is this who hides counsel without knowledge?” (cf. 38:2), and answers, “therefore I have uttered that which I didn’t understand.” Arminian readers note Job’s honest admission of limited understanding.

He speaks of “things too wonderful for me.”
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see Job acknowledging the limits of creaturely knowledge before God.

Shared ground: both traditions read this as humility, not as a confession of the hidden sins the friends alleged, and both note that the prologue never charged Job with such sin (1:22; 2:10).

verses.text: You said, ‘Listen, now, and I will speak; I will question you, and you will answer me.’
verses.arminianNotes:
Job recalls the LORD’s words, “Listen, now, and I will speak; I will question you, and you will answer me.” Arminian readers note that he echoes the LORD’s challenge from the whirlwind (cf. 38:3; 40:7).

Job now accepts the place of the one questioned.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see Job receiving God’s questions rather than demanding answers on his own terms.

Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as Job’s acceptance of the LORD’s address, which has changed the shape of his complaint.

verses.text: I had heard of you by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye sees you.
verses.arminianNotes:
“I had heard of you by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye sees you.” Arminian readers note that Job contrasts secondhand knowledge with a personal encounter.

His earlier hope to see God (19:26–27) is answered in a way he had not foreseen.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see a movement from hearsay to encounter, given by God’s self-revelation.

Shared ground: both traditions treat this as the heart of Job’s answer: the LORD has met him, even though the LORD has not explained the scenes of chapters 1–2.

verses.text: Therefore I abhor myself, and repent in dust and ashes.”
verses.arminianNotes:
“Therefore I abhor myself, and repent in dust and ashes.” Arminian readers note that translators and interpreters discuss several options here: that Job abhors himself, retracts his words, relents, or is comforted concerning dust and ashes.

The phrase “dust and ashes” may recall his place among the ashes (2:8) and his lament, “I have become like dust and ashes” (30:19).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise hold more than one reading open, from self-abasement before God to a turning from his lament.

Shared ground: both traditions agree the verse is a humble response to God, avoid reducing it to one slogan, and do not read it as confirming the friends’ charges, since the LORD commends Job in 42:7.
